# Incident Report — STRRAT RAT Infection

**Case:** mta-2024-07-30 | **Evidence:** `2024-07-30-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (11,562 packets, 2024-07-30 06:38:48–06:48:34 UTC, ~586s) | **Environment:** Windows Active Directory LAN, domain `wiresharkworkshop.online`

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **172.16.1.66** |
| MAC address | **00:1e:64:ec:f3:08** |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-SKBR25F** (NetBIOS: WIRESHARKWORKSH) |
| Logged-in domain user | **ccollier** |
| OS (self-reported by malware) | Microsoft Windows 11 Pro, 64-bit |
| Domain controller (not infected) | 172.16.1.4, WIRESHARK-WS-DC (MAC 5c:f9:dd:8c:97:35) |

Identity was cross-confirmed via NBNS name registrations, Kerberos AS-REQ `CNameString` values (`ccollier`, `DESKTOP-SKBR25F$`), and ARP.

## 2. Malware Family

**STRRAT** — a Java-based remote access trojan (credential stealer, keylogger, fake-ransomware note).

**Attribution: signature-confirmed.** The infected host beacons to its C2 over a raw (non-TLS) TCP socket with a plaintext, pipe-delimited protocol that contains the literal string `STRRAT`:

```
ping|STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|Microsoft Windows 11 Pro|64-bit|Windows Defender|<base64 active-window title>|1.6|US:United States|Not Installed|<uptime>
```

Fields decode to: malware name, campaign ID, hostname, username, OS, architecture, installed AV product, base64-encoded active window title (keylogger/screen-tracking feature — observed values include `Documents`, `Pictures`, `Home`, `Program Manager`, `Fanad Head Lighthouse - Paint`), malware version (**1.6**), country, install/persistence status (`Not Installed`), and infection uptime counter. This is the documented STRRAT check-in format, not an inference from behavior alone.

102 beacons observed from frame 9117 (t=78.07s) through frame 11561 (t=585.66s, end of capture), sent at a steady ~5-second interval — the connection was still active when the capture ended.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise

**Command-and-control**
- **141.98.10.79:12132** (TCP) — STRRAT C2 endpoint, stream `tcp.stream==83`, first SYN at t=76.99s (frame 9066), sustained ~509s. No DNS lookup precedes this connection — the C2 IP is hardcoded in the malware.
- Campaign/build ID embedded in beacons: `1BE8292C`

**Malicious/staging domains (from DNS, resolved just before infection)**
- `github.com` → 140.82.113.3
- `objects.githubusercontent.com` → 185.199.110.133 (GitHub raw content CDN — likely stager/payload host)
- `repo1.maven.org` → 199.232.196.209 (Maven Central — likely used to fetch a JRE/Java dependency for the Java-based payload)

These three lookups fire almost simultaneously at t≈63.965s, followed immediately by large encrypted transfers (≈833 KB from GitHub raw content, ≈9 MB combined across three parallel TLS streams to Maven Central), and the STRRAT C2 beacon begins 13 seconds later. This is consistent with a Java-based loader/stager pulling its payload and runtime dependencies before launching STRRAT. Because both downloads are TLS-encrypted (GlobalSign-issued certs observed for the GitHub streams), **no file names or file hashes are recoverable from this capture** — the payload itself is not visible in cleartext anywhere in the pcap. I am not fabricating a hash or filename; none is present in the evidence.
- `ip-api.com` → 208.95.112.1 — plaintext HTTP GET `/json/` at t=78.01s (frame 9111), immediately after the C2 connection opens and just before the first beacon reports `US:United States`. This is the malware's self-geolocation check, not a legitimate user request (User-Agent spoofs Chrome 73 on Win10, inconsistent with the real Win11 host reported in the STRRAT beacon).

**What the capture does NOT show**
- The initial delivery/infection vector (phishing email, malicious document, drive-by page) is not present — the capture begins with an already-running, benign-looking AD workstation, and the first sign of compromise is the github.com/repo1.maven.org DNS burst at t=63.965s.
- No transferred file names or SHA256 hashes could be extracted; all payload delivery traffic is TLS-encrypted.

## 4. Recommended Actions
- Isolate 172.16.1.66 from the network immediately; treat as fully compromised (STRRAT harvests browser/email credentials).
- Force credential reset for `ccollier` and any accounts cached/used on that host.
- Block egress to 141.98.10.79:12132 at the perimeter/EDR.
- Hunt other hosts for beacons to 141.98.10.79 or the campaign ID `1BE8292C`.
- Acquire host-based forensics (disk/memory) from DESKTOP-SKBR25F to recover the actual STRRAT JAR/loader and obtain a hash, since the network capture alone cannot provide one.
